title: Preterm labour and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Threatened and established preterm labour and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (P-PROM) in India: diagnosis, antibiotics for P-PROM, tocolysis, antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection, place of birth and newborn readiness, using WHO antenatal corticosteroid recommendations (2022) and NICE NG25 because the MoHFW antenatal corticosteroid guideline could not be opened.
findings: Speculum diagnosis of P-PROM, oral erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for up to 10 days, no co-amoxiclav, cervical length 15 mm and fetal fibronectin 50 ng/mL thresholds from 30 weeks, nifedipine tocolysis 26–33+6 weeks, oxytocin receptor antagonist if nifedipine contraindicated, no betamimetics, corticosteroids 24–33+6 weeks with one repeat course, magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 15 minutes then 1 g/hour up to 24 hours at 24–29+6 weeks (consider to 33+6) with 4-hourly monitoring checked against NICE NG25.

Dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses or betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses at 24–34 weeks when birth is likely within 7 days, with gestation reasonably assessed and facilities for newborn care, checked against WHO 2022 recommendations 1.0–1.10.

Nifedipine 20 mg orally then 10–20 mg three to four times daily adjusted to uterine activity (GPnotebook, NICE); intrapartum GBS prophylaxis with benzylpenicillin 3 g IV then 1.8 g IV every 4 hours, cefuroxime 1.5 g for non-severe allergy and vancomycin 20 mg/kg for severe allergy (Louth Hospitals, HSE 2023).
unverifiedSections: The MoHFW Operational Guidelines on antenatal corticosteroids (2014) were not opened.
NICE NG25 names an oral penicillin as the alternative to erythromycin without a regimen; no row is shown, and the choice is left to the obstetrician.
Nifedipine dosing is from a GPnotebook summary of NICE guidance, and GBS prophylaxis from an Irish hospital guideline citing the HSE 2023 national guideline.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: India has the largest number of preterm births in the world, and prematurity is the leading cause of newborn death. Care aims to confirm preterm labour or membrane rupture, buy time for corticosteroids and in-utero transfer to a facility with newborn care, protect the baby's brain with magnesium sulfate before early preterm birth, and prevent infection after membranes rupture. Tocolysis is short-term only. WHO links corticosteroid use to conditions that make it safe: reliable gestational age, birth expected within 7 days, no maternal infection, and adequate care for the preterm baby. Group B streptococcus (GBS) colonisation adds to the risk of early-onset neonatal sepsis, so women in preterm labour receive intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Every hour gained before birth helps, because it allows steroids and transfer.
keyMechanisms: Infection, inflammation, overdistension and bleeding trigger preterm labour.
Corticosteroids speed fetal lung maturation and reduce respiratory distress, brain bleed and death.
Magnesium sulfate reduces cerebral palsy risk in very preterm babies.
After membranes rupture, ascending infection (chorioamnionitis) threatens mother and baby.

physicalSigns: Pooling of amniotic fluid on speculum (NICE)
Maternal tachycardia above 100/min or fetal tachycardia (chorioamnionitis)
redFlags: Chorioamnionitis: fever, tachycardia, uterine tenderness (corticosteroids contraindicated in clinical infection, WHO)
precipitants: Short cervix, anaemia, low maternal weight

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Irregular, painless tightenings with no cervical change; from 30 weeks, cervical length above 15 mm or fibronectin 50 ng/mL or less makes preterm labour unlikely (NICE).
Leak with coughing or a thin discharge but no pooling of liquor on speculum; speculum examination settles it (NICE).
Constant pain, a tender hard uterus and bleeding, sometimes concealed; clinical findings and fetal monitoring settle it (see Antepartum haemorrhage topic).
Dysuria, loin pain and fever; urine microscopy and culture settle it, and infection may itself trigger preterm labour.
Fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and offensive liquor after membrane rupture; clinical diagnosis with raised white cells and CRP.

differentials.condition: Appendicitis or other surgical cause in pregnancy
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Localised right-sided pain and tenderness with anorexia; ultrasound settles it.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Cervical length 15 mm or less, or fetal fibronectin above 50 ng/mL.
24–34 weeks, birth likely within 7 days, no clinical infection, care available for the preterm newborn.
24–29+6 weeks (consider to 33+6) in established labour or planned birth within 24 hours.

ruleIn.testName: Maternal temperature and pulse, white cells, CRP and cardiotocography (CTG); urine culture
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Diagnose intrauterine infection with clinical assessment plus CRP, white cells and CTG together; never use one test alone (NICE 1.5.1–1.5.3).

ruleOut.testName: Insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 or placental alpha-microglobulin-1 test

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm and assess
actions: Gestation, contractions, cervix, membranes, infection, fetal wellbeing (NICE).
Transfer in utero to a facility with newborn care when possible.
Dysuria or bacteriuria: send urine culture and treat urinary infection with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic guided by culture (see the urinary tract infection topic).

clinicalManagement.title: P-PROM
actions: Erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for up to 10 days or until labour (NICE 1.4.1).

Suspected intrauterine infection (fever with raised white cells, fetal tachycardia or offensive liquor): IV ampicillin plus gentamicin, no tocolysis, expedite birth and inform the neonatal team (NICE 1.5; MSD Manual).

clinicalManagement.title: Corticosteroids and tocolysis
actions: Corticosteroids at 24–34 weeks when criteria are met (WHO 2022; NICE 1.9).
Nifedipine 20 mg then 10–20 mg three to four times daily at 26–33+6 weeks with intact membranes; oxytocin receptor antagonist if nifedipine contraindicated; no betamimetics (NICE 1.8; GPnotebook).
At 22+0 to 23+6 weeks, discuss corticosteroids with the woman, family and multidisciplinary team (NICE 1.9.1).
Consider one repeat course before 34+0 weeks if the first was over 7 days ago and birth is very likely within 48 hours; never more than 2 courses (NICE 1.9.4–1.9.5).

clinicalManagement.title: Neuroprotection
actions: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 15 minutes, then 1 g/hour until birth or 24 hours (NICE 1.10.4).
Check pulse, BP, respiratory rate and reflexes at least 4-hourly (NICE 1.10.5).

clinicalManagement.title: Birth
actions: Newborn resuscitation team present; delayed cord clamping where appropriate; thermal care and early breastfeeding (see newborn topics).
Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis with benzylpenicillin when indicated by risk factors (Louth Hospitals; HSE 2023).

vignette.text: Sunita, a 23-year-old primigravida at 30 weeks and 2 days by first-trimester scan, attends a district hospital in Odisha with 4 hours of regular painful tightenings every 7 minutes and lower backache. She has had burning urination for 3 days. Temperature is 37.4°C, BP 112/70 mmHg and pulse 92/min. Speculum shows no pooling of liquor and the cervix appears to be opening. The hospital has no neonatal intensive care unit; the nearest is 90 km away.

guidedApproach.title: Why preterm birth happens and why time matters
guidedApproach.prompt: What can we change once preterm labour starts?
guidedApproach.guidance: Preterm labour is the final common pathway of several processes: infection and inflammation (including urinary and ascending genital infection), overdistension from multiple pregnancy, placental bleeding, cervical insufficiency and maternal stress. Once labour is established it is difficult to stop, and tocolytics only delay birth for a few days. That delay is valuable because it allows two things that change the baby's outcome: a course of corticosteroids, which matures the fetal lungs and reduces respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and death, and transfer of the mother to a hospital with newborn care. Magnesium sulfate given shortly before a very preterm birth protects the fetal brain and reduces cerebral palsy. After the membranes rupture, ascending infection becomes the main threat to both mother and baby.

guidedApproach.title: Recognising true preterm labour and its complications
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you tell real preterm labour from false alarms?
guidedApproach.guidance: Regular painful contractions with progressive cervical change define preterm labour. Before 30 weeks, NICE advises treating suspected preterm labour as real because the cost of missing it is high. From 30 weeks, a transvaginal cervical length of 15 mm or less, or a fetal fibronectin above 50 ng/mL, confirms it, and values above these thresholds make it unlikely. A speculum examination looking for pooled liquor diagnoses P-PROM; digital examination should be avoided after membrane rupture. Look actively for causes and complications: urinary infection, bleeding from abruption, and chorioamnionitis — maternal fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and offensive liquor — which is a contraindication to tocolysis and to delaying birth.

guidedApproach.title: Tests that guide decisions
guidedApproach.guidance: Gestational age must be reliably known before giving corticosteroids, so check the dating scan. Cervical length and fetal fibronectin help from 30 weeks but should not be combined. Urine microscopy and culture look for a treatable trigger. After P-PROM, monitor maternal temperature, pulse, white cell count and CRP for chorioamnionitis, and use fetal heart rate monitoring throughout. An obstetric ultrasound confirms presentation, liquor volume and estimated weight, which help plan the place and mode of birth, and confirms whether in-utero transfer is still safe.

guidedApproach.title: Buying time and protecting the baby
guidedApproach.prompt: What should be given, and in what order?
guidedApproach.guidance: For P-PROM, start erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for up to 10 days and avoid co-amoxiclav because of an association with necrotising enterocolitis. Give corticosteroids — dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for four doses or betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for two doses — at 24–34 weeks when birth is likely within 7 days and there is no clinical infection. With intact membranes at 26–33+6 weeks, nifedipine 20 mg followed by 10–20 mg three to four times daily delays birth long enough to complete steroids and transfer; betamimetics should not be used. When birth is expected within 24 hours at 24–29+6 weeks (consider up to 33+6), give magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 15 minutes then 1 g/hour, monitoring reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. In established preterm labour, give benzylpenicillin for group B streptococcus and call the neonatal team.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 23-year-old woman at 30+2 weeks has regular painful contractions every 7 minutes, intact membranes and a cervical length of 12 mm. She has no fever, bleeding or signs of infection. Her BP is 112/70 mmHg. The nearest neonatal intensive care unit is 90 km away.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.explanation: Betamimetics should not be used for tocolysis (NICE 1.8.5).
Correct. Cervical length 15 mm or less confirms preterm labour; steroids at 24–34 weeks and nifedipine at 26–33+6 weeks buy time for transfer (NICE; WHO).
Erythromycin is for P-PROM; her membranes are intact.
Preterm labour itself is not an indication for caesarean birth.

options.text: Send home with advice as the cervix is closed
options.explanation: A cervical length of 12 mm confirms preterm labour.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Manage confirmed preterm labour with intact membranes.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 28-year-old woman at 31 weeks reports a gush of clear fluid 6 hours ago. Speculum shows pooling of liquor. She is afebrile with pulse 84/min, the uterus is non-tender, and the fetal heart rate is 140/min. She is not contracting.
boardQuestions.question: Which antibiotic should be started?

options.explanation: Co-amoxiclav should not be offered in P-PROM (NICE 1.4.3).
Prophylactic antibiotics are offered after P-PROM (NICE 1.4.1).
This is not the recommended P-PROM prophylaxis and adds unnecessary broad-spectrum exposure.

options.text: Erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for up to 10 days or until established labour
options.explanation: Correct. Erythromycin for up to 10 days or until established labour is the NICE recommendation (1.4.1).
Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is for labour; P-PROM prophylaxis is erythromycin.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: P-PROM: erythromycin 250 mg four times daily up to 10 days; never co-amoxiclav.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 26-year-old woman at 27 weeks is in established preterm labour with the cervix 6 cm dilated. Birth is expected within a few hours. She received the first dose of dexamethasone 2 hours ago. Her reflexes are normal and urine output is adequate.
boardQuestions.question: Which additional treatment protects the baby's brain?

options.explanation: Tocolysis is not appropriate in advanced labour, and it does not protect the brain.
She is already receiving her first course; a repeat course does not protect the brain.

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 15 minutes then 1 g/hour
options.explanation: Correct. Offer magnesium sulfate at 24–29+6 weeks when birth is expected within 24 hours (NICE 1.10.2, 1.10.4).
Not recommended in the cited sources and does not provide neuroprotection.
Phenobarbitone has no role in fetal neuroprotection in the cited sources.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Give magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Birth within 24 hours at 24–29+6 weeks: magnesium sulfate 4 g then 1 g/hour.

patientEducation: Report leaking fluid, fever, bleeding or reduced movements at once.
Explain why corticosteroids and magnesium are given.
